content.title: After Six Years: When the Events Form One Picture
paragraphs: Chapter Twenty
After Six Years: When the Events Form One Picture
Abdullah ibn Suhayl and a Review of the First Stage of the Mission
1. Abdullah ibn Suhayl: Faith, Migration, and Steadfastness

Abdullah ibn Suhayl ibn Amr, may Allah be pleased with him, was among the members of Suhayl’s family who emigrated to Abyssinia, but his story extended beyond that migration. His father Suhayl was a leading man of Banu Amir ibn Lu’ayy and a prominent Qurayshi opponent of the Prophet’s mission. Abdullah took a different path and became one of the early Muslims. Reports differ over whether he joined the first or second migration; the second is the better-known view, while his migration to Abyssinia itself is recorded in the Seerah and biographical works. He was still young. If the reports that he was twenty-seven at Badr are correct, he most likely accepted Islam at around fifteen to seventeen.

When Abdullah returned from Abyssinia, his father did not leave him alone. Ibn Sa’d relates that Suhayl bound and confined him, pressuring him to abandon Islam. Abdullah remained under his father’s authority until Badr several years later. He went out with the Qurayshi army because he was with his father and under his control, not because he had returned to their religion. As the two armies drew near, he found his opportunity: before the fighting began, he crossed over to the Muslims, reached the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, and fought at Badr as a Muslim. His father stood in the Qurayshi army while he stood in the Messenger’s ranks.

Abdullah accompanied the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, in the events after Badr. At the Conquest of Makkah, his father Suhayl ibn Amr embraced Islam. Biographical works relate that Abdullah sought protection for his father. The son once confined by his father because of Islam thus helped secure his safety when circumstances changed. Abdullah lived beyond the Prophet’s death until the Battle of al-Yamamah, fought against Musaylimah’s followers during the caliphate of Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, and was martyred there. Ibn Sa’d reports that Abu Bakr later met Suhayl and offered condolences for his son. His journey had begun as a young believer in an opponent’s household, taken him through migration and confinement to the Prophet’s side at Badr, and allowed him to witness his father’s conversion before he died a martyr.
Further Accounts from Abyssinia
2. Why Did the Negus Say That Allah Had Taken No Bribe from Him?

A Seerah report relates that when the Negus refused Quraysh’s gifts, he explained that Allah had restored his kingdom without taking a bribe from him, so he would not accept a bribe in this matter. This statement was connected to his youth and his recovery of the throne.

Ibn Ishaq relates, in a report transmitted by Urwah ibn al-Zubayr from Aishah, may Allah be pleased with her, that the Negus's father had been king of Abyssinia and had no child besides this boy. The Negus had an uncle who had several sons. Some people of Abyssinia feared that after his father, the kingship would remain dependent on a single heir, so they killed his father and placed his uncle on the throne.

The young Negus grew up under his uncle. His intelligence and firmness gave him considerable influence, which alarmed those who had murdered his father. They feared that his uncle would appoint him king and that he would kill them in revenge, since he already knew they had killed his father. They asked the uncle to kill him or expel him. The uncle refused to kill him but sent him out of the country. According to the report, they sold him to a merchant for six hundred dirhams, and the merchant took him away.

Then, according to the same report, his uncle died that very day. Affairs in Abyssinia became unstable, and none of the uncle's sons proved capable of managing the kingdom properly. The people then began searching for the young man whom they had driven away. They caught up with him, brought him back to Abyssinia, placed the crown on his head, and made him their king.

But the merchant who had paid for him came demanding his right. The people tried to withhold the merchant’s money. According to the report, the Negus required them either to repay what the merchant had paid or to hand over the young man he had purchased so that he could take him wherever he wished—even though that young man was now their king. As king, he could have ignored the transaction, but he did not. The merchant’s money was returned.

This incident explains the Negus’s refusal of Quraysh’s gifts years later. He understood that Allah had restored his kingdom without his buying it through bribery; he would therefore not accept gifts as a price for changing his judgment about those who had sought refuge with him. These details belong to historical Seerah reports, not all of which are established at the level of authentic hadith. They are therefore distinct from the authenticated reports in the Sahih collections of al-Bukhari and Muslim.
3. Another Challenge Faced by the Negus

The Negus faced another trial, different from the earlier attempt by a rival to seize his kingdom. This dispute concerned his beliefs rather than who would rule Abyssinia. Ibn Ishaq relates that a group of Abyssinians accused him of abandoning their religion after he accepted what the Muslims said about Jesus, peace be upon him, and rose against him. Recognizing the danger, he sent for Ja’far and his companions and prepared ships for them. According to the report, he instructed them to leave for a place of safety if he was defeated, and to remain if he prevailed.

He then wrote a statement testifying that there is no deity worthy of worship except Allah, that Muhammad is His servant and Messenger, and that Jesus is His servant and Messenger, His word, and a spirit from Him. The spirit here is one created by Allah and attributed to Him as an honor; it does not mean that Jesus, peace be upon him, is part of Allah. He placed the document close to his chest and went out to his people.

First he asked them about his conduct among them. They testified that he had ruled them well. Then they told him that their objection concerned Jesus, peace be upon him. He asked what they themselves said about Jesus, and they stated their belief. The Negus then placed his hand on his chest over the concealed document and affirmed his testimony concerning Jesus son of Mary, peace be upon him. He meant the belief he had written down, without spelling it out to them. The people understood his words differently, were satisfied, and withdrew.

This too is a historical Seerah report whose details do not carry the standing of an authenticated hadith. It depicts the personal danger that protecting the Muslims could entail for the Negus. He governed a society with its own creed and internal powers, where religious disagreement could become a threat to the ruler himself.
The First Six Years of the Mission

After the accounts of migration to Abyssinia, the Seerah reaches approximately the end of the fifth year or the beginning of the sixth year of the mission. Taken together, the accounts of persecution, migration, and negotiations with Quraysh reveal patterns that are less apparent when each event is considered alone.
4. Makkan Trials in the History of Revelation

Revelation taught the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, from the beginning that earlier messengers had faced trials like his. In those first days, Waraqah ibn Nawfal explained that the one who had come to Muhammad was Gabriel, the angel who had come to Moses, peace be upon them, and that anyone bringing a message like his had faced hostility. The Qur’an continued to reinforce this meaning from different angles.
Allah says:
There were messengers rejected before you, but they endured patiently their rejection and persecution until Our help came to them.
— Al-An'am 6:34. — Rowwad Translation Center (excerpt)

The Makkan events followed recurring patterns that Allah describes in the lives of messengers, peoples, and human societies. A messenger brings the truth, his people differ over him, the evidence becomes clear, denial follows, and the believers face trials and are commanded to be patient. The Qur’an thus places the Muslims’ experience within a long history of revelation, rather than leaving them to understand it as though such trials had begun with them.
5. Continuing to Present Evidence despite Rejection

Despite Quraysh’s persistent denial, the Qur’an continued to address them, presenting arguments, questions, and evidence repeatedly, answering their objections and correcting the falsehood within them.

Who created? Who provides? Who gives life and causes death? What evidence is there that idols deserve any share of worship? How can resurrection be denied when the human being was created the first time? What happened to peoples who rejected their messengers?

The conflict did not become mere confrontation at the first denial. Long years of explaining the truth through evidence and answering doubts preceded and accompanied it. The same pattern recurs in the Makkan surahs: people deny and further verses come; they argue and receive another answer; they demand a sign and are answered; they mock, yet the explanation continues. Forbearance, allowing time, and presenting evidence in different ways were central to this period.
6. Divine Choice Does Not Follow Human Measures
The early years also reveal how Allah chooses whom He wills for His purposes. He chose Muhammad, peace and blessings be upon him, as His Messenger.
Allah says:
Allah knows best where to place His message.
— Al-An'am 6:124. — Rowwad Translation Center (excerpt)
And He says:
Your Lord creates and chooses what He wills…
— Al-Qasas 28:68. — Rowwad Translation Center (excerpt)
It is authentically reported that the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said:
“Allah selected Kinānah from the children of Isma‘īl, Quraysh from Kinānah, the children of Hāshim from Quraysh, and me from the children of Hāshim.”
— Sahih Muslim, 2276. Translation: HadeethEnc, excerpt from the parallel report in Ibn Hibban.

Divine choice in the Seerah extended beyond lineage. Allah chose men and women from different social classes for this message: people from Makkah and elsewhere, from powerful households and vulnerable groups, from the nobility and from clients affiliated with families or tribes through alliance or manumission. Some were people whom Makkan society would not have placed foremost. The earliest believers show that those chosen by Allah were not necessarily those held in high esteem by society.
7. Firmness in the Message, Flexibility in the Means

The message remained unchanged, while the means of conveying and protecting it could differ. When compromise over creed was proposed, there was no room to alter the foundation of the message. When the Muslims stood before the Negus, they did not change what they believed about Jesus, peace be upon him, in order to guarantee their stay.

At the same time, Muslims made use of lawful means that could protect them: tribal protection, a just ruler, migration to a safe country, concealment when necessary, and other available means. Being realistic did not mean changing the religion. Remaining firm in the religion did not mean rejecting the lawful means available to them.
8. The Qur’an Accompanies and Explains Events

The revelation of the Qur’an accompanied this entire period. The Companions did not live through events and then read their explanation decades later; verses came while they were facing those events. Revelation answered denial, verses of patience accompanied suffering, the Qur’an exposed the reality behind polytheist claims, and a crisis was placed within a wider history than its immediate moment.

In this way the Qur’an strengthened that generation. It taught them both what to believe and how to understand what was happening to them. A person’s ability to endure changes when he understands where an event stands in relation to truth and falsehood, why such trials occur, what preceded them in the lives of the messengers, and what Allah has promised beyond them.
Who Carried the Message During Those Years?
9. Teaching the Companions to Take Responsibility

The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, nurtured people able to act responsibly both in his presence and far from him. Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, was a means through which several of the earliest Muslims entered Islam. Ja'far, may Allah be pleased with him, led the emigrants in Abyssinia while the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, remained in Makkah. Other Companions assumed different responsibilities according to the needs of the time.

The Prophet’s teaching did not leave his followers dependent on his physical presence before they could act. It developed people who understood the foundation of the message and each assumed as much responsibility as they were able.
10. A Remarkably Young Generation
Many who bore the burdens of the first years were boys and young men without long experience of life, including Abdullah ibn Suhayl.

Al-Zubayr ibn al-Awwam was among the younger early Muslims, yet in Abyssinia he was entrusted with going out to learn the outcome of the fighting that threatened the stability of the Negus’s rule. Al-Arqam ibn Abi al-Arqam was a young man, and his house became one of the best-known meeting places of the Muslims in the early period. Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, entered Islam at a young age. Young people were already taking part in those difficult years; their role did not begin only after the hardship had passed.
11. Women Were Central to the Early Community

Khadijah, may Allah be pleased with her, was part of the story from its very first moment. Sumayyah, may Allah be pleased with her, was among the earliest to give her life because of faith. Women took part in the migration. Some enslaved and vulnerable women were also subjected to harm.

Women were therefore not a secondary addition that appeared after the Muslim community had become established. They were present at the heart of the founding years: in believing, in strengthening others, in being tested, in migration, and in building Muslim family life away from Makkah.
12. Patience and Lawful Means of Protection

Patience was one of the greatest themes of the period. But the events themselves show that patience was not an invitation to seek suffering. When harm could be removed through a lawful means, that means was used. When an enslaved person could be freed from the hand of someone torturing him or her, manumission became a way of rescue. When movement to a safe country became possible, migration took place. When remaining openly visible was unsafe, concealment and caution were used.

Thus two things existed together without contradiction: steadfastness when a trial arrives, and seeking to repel it when a lawful way exists. This is different from imagining patience to mean that a person must continue to suffer harm even when a legitimate path out is available.
13. Caution and Trust in Allah

From the early days of the mission, Muslims learned that knowing the truth did not mean revealing every movement to their opponents. There was a period when the polytheists did not know everyone who had entered Islam. Meetings included a degree of concealment. A Muslim had to know when to appear, when to be cautious, when public declaration was beneficial, and when it would cause unnecessary harm.

The precise reasons for choosing al-Arqam’s house as the meeting place are not all known with certainty. Various explanations have been given, but not all are supported by evidence. Caution, vigilance, and practical precautions were compatible with trust in Allah and formed part of how that generation carried the mission.
14. The Qur'an Taught the Believers How to Understand Their Opponents

The Qur’an did more than expose the falsehood of the opponents’ position. It showed the believers how their opponents objected, denied, and obstructed the truth. It reported their claims and answered them, at times uncovering the pride or stubborn denial behind an objection, and showed how doubts could be used to stop others from listening to the truth.

A Companion learned what he believed, what his opponent claimed, where that claim came from, and how the Qur’an answered it. This relationship between revelation and events was part of the education described in the Seerah. Its full significance cannot be understood by separating political and social events from the surahs revealed at the time.
A New Measure of People
15. The Person Society Does Not Notice May Be Mentioned by the Qur'an
Quraysh measured people by lineage, wealth, protection, and status. Revelation created another measure.
Allah says:
Do not send away [O Prophet] those who invoke their Lord morning and evening, seeking His Face [pleasure].
— Al-An'am 6:52. — Rowwad Translation Center (excerpt)

There were Muslims who possessed nothing that would make Quraysh give them a place of honor in its gatherings. But their lack of importance in society's scale did not mean a lack of importance before Allah. The same idea appears in the story of Abdullah ibn Umm Maktum, may Allah be pleased with him, the blind man whose coming to the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, is associated by the well-known exegetical view with the opening of Surah Abasa:
He frowned and turned away, when the blind man came to him.
— Abasa 80:1–2. — Rowwad Translation Center

At that moment, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was intent on inviting leading men of Quraysh to Islam, hoping that they would accept it. Yet the divine correction came concerning a man whom Quraysh's measures did not place in the same rank as those leaders. Quraysh asks: What is this man's standing among people? The scale formed by revelation asks: How has he turned toward Allah and the truth?
16. The Houses of the Fiercest Opponents Were Not Closed to Guidance

Many believers came from the households of men who actively resisted the mission. They embraced Islam in its earliest days, before the Conquest of Makkah made Muslim power evident. Hisham ibn al-As came from the household of al-As ibn Wa’il; Abu Hudhayfah from that of Utbah ibn Rabi’ah; Umm Habibah, may Allah be pleased with her, from that of Abu Sufyan; and Abdullah and others from that of Suhayl ibn Amr. Sons, daughters, and relatives from other households known for opposing the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, also became Muslims early on.

A father's position does not determine his son's. A household's reputation does not determine the heart of every person within it. The intensity of one man's hostility toward the truth does not mean that goodness will never emerge from his family. A person observing the mission at its beginning therefore could not divide families into families with no hope of accepting Islam and families likely to do so merely by looking at their leading men.
Surah Fussilat in Its Makkan Setting
17. Understanding the Surah through Its Context

These themes appear in Surah Fussilat, which the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, recited to Utbah ibn Rabi’ah when he came to negotiate. Understanding its Makkan setting—denial, persecution, migration, attempted compromise, and the continued presentation of evidence despite rejection—makes the surah’s connection to this period clearer. Its opening brings these themes together:

Hā Mīm. A revelation from the Most Compassionate, the Most Merciful, a Book whose verses are well explained; an Arabic Qur’an for people who understand, as a bearer of glad tidings and a warner; yet most of them turn away and they do not listen.
— Fussilat 41:1–4. — Rowwad Translation Center
The verses describe clear revelation that brings good news and warning, followed by people turning away. These meanings have concrete examples in the preceding Makkan events.
18. Earlier Messengers Faced the Same Hostility
The surah moves through signs of creation, warnings to those who deny, and the story of the ancient peoples of Ad and Thamud, then returns to the point Waraqah ibn Nawfal had already made:
Nothing is said to you [O Prophet] except what was already said to the messengers before you.
— Fussilat 41:43. — Rowwad Translation Center (excerpt)

What Muhammad, peace and blessings be upon him, was hearing from his people was not new in the history of revelation. The stories of the prophets in the Qur'an therefore became part of strengthening the Prophet and his Companions, not merely information about the past.
19. Steadfastness in the Lives of the Believers
In the same surah, Allah says:
Those who say, “Our Lord is Allah,” then remain steadfast, the angels will descend upon them [saying], “Do not fear, nor grieve, but receive glad tidings of Paradise which you were promised. […]”
— Fussilat 41:30, from the angelic address in 41:30–32. Rowwad Translation Center. […] marks the omitted continuation.
The first six years of the Seerah show how this description of steadfastness took form in people’s lives:
“then remain steadfast”

Steadfastness took practical form in the lives of those who chose faith and bore its consequences. Some lost their family’s protection, left their homeland, endured pressure from relatives, or spent years in a foreign land. Their experiences illustrate the verse’s meaning, while the verse explains the place of those experiences on the path of faith.
20. A Firm Message without Imitating Its Opponents
The surah then says:
Who is better in speech than one who calls to Allah, does righteous deeds, and says, “I am one of the Muslims [submitting to Allah]”? Good and evil are not equal. Repel evil with what is good;
— Fussilat 41:33–34. — Rowwad Translation Center (excerpt)

Muhammad ibn Sirin is reported to have understood the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, as foremost among those described here. The verse nevertheless applies generally to anyone who calls to Allah and acts righteously:
Who is better in speech than one who calls to Allah, does righteous deeds, and says, “I am one of the Muslims [submitting to Allah]”?
Facing hostility did not require the Muslims to imitate their opponents’ conduct. Remaining firm in the truth was different from adopting the character of those who opposed it.
21. The Evidence Continues to Be Presented

Although Surah Fussilat speaks of the rejection of the polytheists, the stories of peoples who denied their messengers, the thunderbolt, and punishment, it does not end by suggesting that the door of explanation has been closed.
Near its conclusion Allah says:
We will show them Our signs in the universe and in their own selves until it becomes clear to them that this [Qur’an] is the truth. Is it not enough that your Lord is a Witness over all things?
— Fussilat 41:53. — Rowwad Translation Center
Despite the denial and suffering, this promise remained:
“We will show them Our signs”
The explanation continues, the signs multiply, and the evidence is renewed.
22. What Had These Years Produced?

The Muslims did not yet have a state; Badr had not occurred; Quraysh continued to oppose them; and many Muslims were still in Abyssinia. Yet those years were more than a wait for a stronger period. They established a foundation of faith that connected believers to the path of the earlier prophets.

The believers learned that clarity in the message was compatible with wisdom in the means, and that the Qur’an explained both what to believe and how to understand their circumstances. Responsibility did not depend on reaching old age; women had participated in the mission from its beginning; a person society considered weak could be great before Allah; and even the children of fierce opponents could become early believers.

They combined patience with practical means, firmness without recklessness, caution without abandoning the mission, and clarity without losing wisdom. This was the foundation formed over approximately six years.

In the next stage, Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, would embrace Islam after standing among its opponents. His conversion would visibly affect the Muslims’ position in Makkah. The following chapter begins the account of that change.
Primary Sources for This Chapter

The biography of Abdullah ibn Suhayl ibn Amr, may Allah be pleased with him, in the accounts of Ibn Ishaq, Ibn Sa'd, al-Baladhuri, and other biographical works, which differ over whether he joined the first or second migration.

The account of the Negus's upbringing, restoration to kingship, and the background to his statement about bribery: a Seerah report from Ibn Ishaq, transmitted from Urwah ibn al-Zubayr from Aishah, may Allah be pleased with her; it is therefore presented as a Seerah report.

The report that some Abyssinians opposed the Negus because of his position regarding Jesus, peace be upon him: among the Seerah reports transmitted by Ibn Ishaq, without raising its status to that of an authenticated hadith.
The hadith on Allah choosing Kinanah, then Quraysh, then Banu Hashim, then the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him: Sahih Muslim.
Qur'anic passages cited in this chapter: Al-An'am, Al-Qasas, Abasa, and Fussilat.

The same pattern recurs in the Makkan surahs: people deny and further verses come; they argue and receive another answer; they demand a sign and are answered; they mock, yet the explanation continues. Forbearance, allowing time, and presenting evidence in different ways were central to this period.
6. Divine Choice Does Not Follow Human Measures
The early years also reveal how Allah chooses whom He wills for His purposes. He chose Muhammad, peace and blessings be upon him, as His Messenger.
Allah says:
Allah knows best where to place His message.
— Al-An'am 6:124. — Rowwad Translation Center (excerpt)
And He says:
Your Lord creates and chooses what He wills…
— Al-Qasas 28:68. — Rowwad Translation Center (excerpt)
It is authentically reported that the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said:
“Allah selected Kinānah from the children of Isma‘īl, Quraysh from Kinānah, the children of Hāshim from Quraysh, and me from the children of Hāshim.”
— Sahih Muslim, 2276. Translation: HadeethEnc, excerpt from the parallel report in Ibn Hibban.

Divine choice in the Seerah extended beyond lineage. Allah chose men and women from different social classes for this message: people from Makkah and elsewhere, from powerful households and vulnerable groups, from the nobility and from clients affiliated with families or tribes through alliance or manumission. Some were people whom Makkan society would not have placed foremost. The earliest believers show that those chosen by Allah were not necessarily those held in high esteem by society.
7. Firmness in the Message, Flexibility in the Means

The message remained unchanged, while the means of conveying and protecting it could differ. When compromise over creed was proposed, there was no room to alter the foundation of the message. When the Muslims stood before the Negus, they did not change what they believed about Jesus, peace be upon him, in order to guarantee their stay.

At the same time, Muslims made use of lawful means that could protect them: tribal protection, a just ruler, migration to a safe country, concealment when necessary, and other available means. Being realistic did not mean changing the religion. Remaining firm in the religion did not mean rejecting the lawful means available to them.
8. The Qur’an Accompanies and Explains Events

The revelation of the Qur’an accompanied this entire period. The Companions did not live through events and then read their explanation decades later; verses came while they were facing those events. Revelation answered denial, verses of patience accompanied suffering, the Qur’an exposed the reality behind polytheist claims, and a crisis was placed within a wider history than its immediate moment.

In this way the Qur’an strengthened that generation. It taught them both what to believe and how to understand what was happening to them. A person’s ability to endure changes when he understands where an event stands in relation to truth and falsehood, why such trials occur, what preceded them in the lives of the messengers, and what Allah has promised beyond them.
Who Carried the Message During Those Years?
9. Teaching the Companions to Take Responsibility

The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, nurtured people able to act responsibly both in his presence and far from him. Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, was a means through which several of the earliest Muslims entered Islam. Ja'far, may Allah be pleased with him, led the emigrants in Abyssinia while the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, remained in Makkah. Other Companions assumed different responsibilities according to the needs of the time.

The Prophet’s teaching did not leave his followers dependent on his physical presence before they could act. It developed people who understood the foundation of the message and each assumed as much responsibility as they were able.
10. A Remarkably Young Generation
Many who bore the burdens of the first years were boys and young men without long experience of life, including Abdullah ibn Suhayl.

Al-Zubayr ibn al-Awwam was among the younger early Muslims, yet in Abyssinia he was entrusted with going out to learn the outcome of the fighting that threatened the stability of the Negus’s rule. Al-Arqam ibn Abi al-Arqam was a young man, and his house became one of the best-known meeting places of the Muslims in the early period. Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, entered Islam at a young age. Young people were already taking part in those difficult years; their role did not begin only after the hardship had passed.
11. Women Were Central to the Early Community

Khadijah, may Allah be pleased with her, was part of the story from its very first moment. Sumayyah, may Allah be pleased with her, was among the earliest to give her life because of faith. Women took part in the migration. Some enslaved and vulnerable women were also subjected to harm.

Women were therefore not a secondary addition that appeared after the Muslim community had become established. They were present at the heart of the founding years: in believing, in strengthening others, in being tested, in migration, and in building Muslim family life away from Makkah.
12. Patience and Lawful Means of Protection

Patience was one of the greatest themes of the period. But the events themselves show that patience was not an invitation to seek suffering. When harm could be removed through a lawful means, that means was used. When an enslaved person could be freed from the hand of someone torturing him or her, manumission became a way of rescue. When movement to a safe country became possible, migration took place. When remaining openly visible was unsafe, concealment and caution were used.

Thus two things existed together without contradiction: steadfastness when a trial arrives, and seeking to repel it when a lawful way exists. This is different from imagining patience to mean that a person must continue to suffer harm even when a legitimate path out is available.
13. Caution and Trust in Allah

From the early days of the mission, Muslims learned that knowing the truth did not mean revealing every movement to their opponents. There was a period when the polytheists did not know everyone who had entered Islam. Meetings included a degree of concealment. A Muslim had to know when to appear, when to be cautious, when public declaration was beneficial, and when it would cause unnecessary harm.

The precise reasons for choosing al-Arqam’s house as the meeting place are not all known with certainty. Various explanations have been given, but not all are supported by evidence. Caution, vigilance, and practical precautions were compatible with trust in Allah and formed part of how that generation carried the mission.
14. The Qur'an Taught the Believers How to Understand Their Opponents

The Qur’an did more than expose the falsehood of the opponents’ position. It showed the believers how their opponents objected, denied, and obstructed the truth. It reported their claims and answered them, at times uncovering the pride or stubborn denial behind an objection, and showed how doubts could be used to stop others from listening to the truth.

A Companion learned what he believed, what his opponent claimed, where that claim came from, and how the Qur’an answered it. This relationship between revelation and events was part of the education described in the Seerah. Its full significance cannot be understood by separating political and social events from the surahs revealed at the time.
A New Measure of People
15. The Person Society Does Not Notice May Be Mentioned by the Qur'an
Quraysh measured people by lineage, wealth, protection, and status. Revelation created another measure.
Allah says:
Do not send away [O Prophet] those who invoke their Lord morning and evening, seeking His Face [pleasure].
— Al-An'am 6:52. — Rowwad Translation Center (excerpt)

There were Muslims who possessed nothing that would make Quraysh give them a place of honor in its gatherings. But their lack of importance in society's scale did not mean a lack of importance before Allah. The same idea appears in the story of Abdullah ibn Umm Maktum, may Allah be pleased with him, the blind man whose coming to the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, is associated by the well-known exegetical view with the opening of Surah Abasa:
He frowned and turned away, when the blind man came to him.
— Abasa 80:1–2. — Rowwad Translation Center

At that moment, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was intent on inviting leading men of Quraysh to Islam, hoping that they would accept it. Yet the divine correction came concerning a man whom Quraysh's measures did not place in the same rank as those leaders. Quraysh asks: What is this man's standing among people? The scale formed by revelation asks: How has he turned toward Allah and the truth?
16. The Houses of the Fiercest Opponents Were Not Closed to Guidance

Many believers came from the households of men who actively resisted the mission. They embraced Islam in its earliest days, before the Conquest of Makkah made Muslim power evident. Hisham ibn al-As came from the household of al-As ibn Wa’il; Abu Hudhayfah from that of Utbah ibn Rabi’ah; Umm Habibah, may Allah be pleased with her, from that of Abu Sufyan; and Abdullah and others from that of Suhayl ibn Amr. Sons, daughters, and relatives from other households known for opposing the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, also became Muslims early on.

A father's position does not determine his son's. A household's reputation does not determine the heart of every person within it. The intensity of one man's hostility toward the truth does not mean that goodness will never emerge from his family. A person observing the mission at its beginning therefore could not divide families into families with no hope of accepting Islam and families likely to do so merely by looking at their leading men.
Surah Fussilat in Its Makkan Setting
17. Understanding the Surah through Its Context

These themes appear in Surah Fussilat, which the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, recited to Utbah ibn Rabi’ah when he came to negotiate. Understanding its Makkan setting—denial, persecution, migration, attempted compromise, and the continued presentation of evidence despite rejection—makes the surah’s connection to this period clearer. Its opening brings these themes together:

Hā Mīm. A revelation from the Most Compassionate, the Most Merciful, a Book whose verses are well explained; an Arabic Qur’an for people who understand, as a bearer of glad tidings and a warner; yet most of them turn away and they do not listen.
— Fussilat 41:1–4. — Rowwad Translation Center
The verses describe clear revelation that brings good news and warning, followed by people turning away. These meanings have concrete examples in the preceding Makkan events.
18. Earlier Messengers Faced the Same Hostility
The surah moves through signs of creation, warnings to those who deny, and the story of the ancient peoples of Ad and Thamud, then returns to the point Waraqah ibn Nawfal had already made:
Nothing is said to you [O Prophet] except what was already said to the messengers before you.
— Fussilat 41:43. — Rowwad Translation Center (excerpt)

What Muhammad, peace and blessings be upon him, was hearing from his people was not new in the history of revelation. The stories of the prophets in the Qur'an therefore became part of strengthening the Prophet and his Companions, not merely information about the past.
19. Steadfastness in the Lives of the Believers
In the same surah, Allah says:
Those who say, “Our Lord is Allah,” then remain steadfast, the angels will descend upon them [saying], “Do not fear, nor grieve, but receive glad tidings of Paradise which you were promised. […]”
— Fussilat 41:30, from the angelic address in 41:30–32. Rowwad Translation Center. […] marks the omitted continuation.
The first six years of the Seerah show how this description of steadfastness took form in people’s lives:
“then remain steadfast”

Steadfastness took practical form in the lives of those who chose faith and bore its consequences. Some lost their family’s protection, left their homeland, endured pressure from relatives, or spent years in a foreign land. Their experiences illustrate the verse’s meaning, while the verse explains the place of those experiences on the path of faith.
20. A Firm Message without Imitating Its Opponents
The surah then says:
Who is better in speech than one who calls to Allah, does righteous deeds, and says, “I am one of the Muslims [submitting to Allah]”? Good and evil are not equal. Repel evil with what is good;
— Fussilat 41:33–34. — Rowwad Translation Center (excerpt)

Muhammad ibn Sirin is reported to have understood the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, as foremost among those described here. The verse nevertheless applies generally to anyone who calls to Allah and acts righteously:
Who is better in speech than one who calls to Allah, does righteous deeds, and says, “I am one of the Muslims [submitting to Allah]”?
Facing hostility did not require the Muslims to imitate their opponents’ conduct. Remaining firm in the truth was different from adopting the character of those who opposed it.
21. The Evidence Continues to Be Presented

Although Surah Fussilat speaks of the rejection of the polytheists, the stories of peoples who denied their messengers, the thunderbolt, and punishment, it does not end by suggesting that the door of explanation has been closed.
Near its conclusion Allah says:
We will show them Our signs in the universe and in their own selves until it becomes clear to them that this [Qur’an] is the truth. Is it not enough that your Lord is a Witness over all things?
— Fussilat 41:53. — Rowwad Translation Center
Despite the denial and suffering, this promise remained:
“We will show them Our signs”
The explanation continues, the signs multiply, and the evidence is renewed.
22. What Had These Years Produced?

The Muslims did not yet have a state; Badr had not occurred; Quraysh continued to oppose them; and many Muslims were still in Abyssinia. Yet those years were more than a wait for a stronger period. They established a foundation of faith that connected believers to the path of the earlier prophets.

The believers learned that clarity in the message was compatible with wisdom in the means, and that the Qur’an explained both what to believe and how to understand their circumstances. Responsibility did not depend on reaching old age; women had participated in the mission from its beginning; a person society considered weak could be great before Allah; and even the children of fierce opponents could become early believers.

They combined patience with practical means, firmness without recklessness, caution without abandoning the mission, and clarity without losing wisdom. This was the foundation formed over approximately six years.

In the next stage, Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, would embrace Islam after standing among its opponents. His conversion would visibly affect the Muslims’ position in Makkah. The following chapter begins the account of that change.
